Fig. 10: Good news in the DSGE model: sticky prices

Goal. Compare the same good news with sticky prices (textbook Exercise 1(d)).

With sticky prices, firms supply whatever is demanded. The good news raises consumption, so firms must produce more and need more workers: the vertical labor demand curve shifts right, from \(Y_0 = 1\) to \(Y' = 1.1\). At the same time labor supply still shifts up, because people feel richer. Firms must pay a higher wage to get the labor they need. Use the buttons (in Colab) or the slider (on the website) to switch between the two cases.

# Fig. 10: the function of Fig. 9, with the sticky-prices button selected
interact(
    good_news,
    c_new=FloatSlider(value=0.7, min=0.5, max=0.8, step=0.05,
                      description="consumption after the news c′", style=WIDE),
    prices=ToggleButtons(options=["flexible", "sticky"], value="sticky",
                         description="prices"),
);
Show the code of the website version 
# @title Website version: Fig. 10 with a slider between flexible and sticky prices
# a slider with two steps: flexible prices, then sticky prices
slider_figure(
    good_news,
    "prices",
    ["flexible", "sticky"],
    start="sticky",
    label="prices",
)

Source. Adapted from Fig. 15.15 in Jones (2024), Macroeconomics, 6th ed., which illustrates the worked solution to its Exercise 1.

What to notice.

  • With sticky prices, employment rises, from 1.00 to 1.15, and the real wage rises a lot, from 0.67 to 0.90. With flexible prices (Fig. 9) employment fell to 0.89.
  • The same shock moves employment in opposite directions depending on whether prices are sticky. This is why macroeconomists argue so much about how sticky prices really are.

Your turn. Textbook Exercise 4: government purchases fall for a while. Households expect lower taxes, so consumption rises to 0.65, but total demand falls, to \(Y' = 0.95\). With sticky prices, what happens to employment and to the real wage? Use sticky_prices(Y_new=0.95, c_new=0.65).

Hint

The vertical demand curve moves left and labor supply moves up. Employment clearly falls; for the real wage the two shifts pull in opposite directions. The title rounds both wages to 0.67, so print them with more decimals: compare supply_wage(labor_needed(0.95), 0.65) with w0.

15.8 Concluding remarks

  • DSGE models are dynamic (they trace the economy over time), stochastic (shocks hit it) and general equilibrium (prices clear the markets). Their shocks fade as impulse responses, equation (1), and adjustment costs delay their peak effects.
  • They grew out of real business cycle models, which added TFP shocks to the Solow model, equation (2). TFP is measured as a Solow residual, equation (3); U.S. TFP growth swings a lot, but once utilization is removed, equation (4), it does not fall in most recessions.
  • The labor market is a key block of every DSGE model. Labor demand and supply, equations (5) and (6), give employment and the wage in equation (7). With consumption taken as given, a TFP fall or a sales tax lowers employment and the wage together, like a recession; a rise in government purchases or good news acts through consumption and labor supply instead.
  • Nominal rigidities decide how monetary policy works. With sticky wages, equation (8), an expansion raises employment but lowers the real wage; with sticky prices, equation (9), labor demand is vertical and an expansion raises both. Estimated DSGE models such as Smets–Wouters are quantitative: their impulse response functions say how much and how fast GDP, consumption, hours and inflation respond to each shock.
  • The next chapter studies consumption itself: the permanent-income hypothesis and the microfoundations behind the consumption that this chapter took as given.
  • For an advanced treatment, Appendix I solves the full Smets–Wouters model in Python and recomputes the impulse responses of textbook Figs. 15.9–15.13.

Practice problems

These ten problems put the chapter’s tools to work: conceptual problems apply its equations to real episodes, data-based problems send you back to Fernald’s data and the Penn World Table, and modeling problems answer policy questions with the labor-market diagrams. Each problem is marked Basic, Intermediate or Challenge. Try it on your own before you open the Hint and the Solution; the sliders of the modeling problems run in Colab (open the notebook with the badge at the top), and on the website you can use the website version of each figure above.

Conceptual problems

Problem 1 (Basic): How long do shocks last in an estimated DSGE model? Smets and Wouters (2007) estimated their model on quarterly U.S. data from 1966 to 2004. Each of its shocks fades like the shock process of the Model overview, \(x_{t+1} = \rho\,x_t + \varepsilon_{t+1}\). The table lists five of their estimates of \(\rho\) (the posterior modes in Table 1b of the working-paper version; the article is doi:10.1257/aer.97.3.586).

Shock What it moves \(\rho\) per quarter
productivity TFP 0.95
government spending public purchases 0.97
investment technology how much new capital each dollar of investment buys 0.71
risk premium the gap between the central bank’s rate and the return households require 0.18
monetary policy the interest rate, beyond what the central bank’s rule prescribes 0.12

  1. Use the half-life formula of the Model overview to compute the half-life of each shock, in quarters.

  2. Use equation (1) to compute the share of each shock that is still left one year (4 quarters) after it hits.

  3. The monetary policy shock is almost gone after a single quarter, yet the chapter reports that GDP falls most 3 to 4 quarters after a monetary shock. Which features of a DSGE model can give a short-lived shock long-lived effects?

Hint

The half-life is \(h = \ln 2/(-\ln\rho)\), and by equation (1) the share left after \(n\) quarters is \(\rho^n\); np.log gives the natural log. For (c), reread the frictions in “The building blocks of a DSGE model”, the adjustment-cost rule after equation (1), and ask how a central bank moves its interest rate from one quarter to the next.

Your answer:

# Your answer here
Solution

(a) and (b). For productivity, \(h = \ln 2/(-\ln 0.95) = 0.6931/0.0513 = 13.5\) quarters, and after a year \(0.95^4 = 0.81\) of the shock is left. The same two steps for every shock give:

Shock \(\rho\) Half-life, quarters Share left after a year, \(\rho^4\)
productivity 0.95 13.5, about 3.4 years 0.81
government spending 0.97 22.8, about 5.7 years 0.89
investment technology 0.71 2.0 0.25
risk premium 0.18 0.40 0.001
monetary policy 0.12 0.33 0.0002

The productivity estimate of 0.95 is close to the \(\rho = 0.958\) that the Model overview derived from a half-life of 16 quarters. In Python:

shocks = {"productivity": 0.95, "government spending": 0.97, "investment technology": 0.71,
          "risk premium": 0.18, "monetary policy": 0.12}
for name, rho_shock in shocks.items():
    half_life = np.log(2) / -np.log(rho_shock)
    print(f"{name:22s} half-life {half_life:5.2f} quarters, left after a year {rho_shock ** 4:.4f}")

shocks.items() walks through the pairs of a dictionary, one name and one value at a time.

(c) A shock and its effects are not the same thing. Three features spread a short shock over many quarters:

  • Adjustment costs. With the rule \(y_t = y_{t-1} + \lambda(x_t - y_{t-1})\), the economy closes only part of the gap each quarter, so its response keeps growing after the shock has faded. With \(\rho = 0.8\) and \(\lambda = 0.3\) it peaks 3 quarters later (the Model overview’s check).
  • Sticky prices and wages. Prices adjust slowly, so a higher nominal interest rate is also a higher real rate for several quarters, and spending stays low.
  • A smooth policy rule. In the estimated rule the interest rate puts a weight of 0.81 on its own value of the quarter before (Table 1a of the same paper), so a rate that jumps comes back down only slowly, long after the shock itself is gone.

So the long swings of a DSGE model come either from shocks that are very persistent themselves (productivity, government spending) or from frictions that stretch short-lived shocks, like the monetary one, over many quarters.

Problem 2 (Intermediate): Two recessions, two stories: 1974 and 1982. John Fernald’s data in tfp_annual.csv (Federal Reserve Bank of San Francisco) give, for the U.S. business sector (percent per year):

Year Output growth Raw Solow residual Utilization
1974 −1.56 −3.72 −2.62
1982 −2.31 −2.76 −2.94

  1. Use equation (4) to compute true TFP growth in each year.

  2. In 1973–74 an oil embargo nearly quadrupled the price of oil, from $2.90 to $11.65 a barrel (Federal Reserve History). Our production function has no oil in it. Explain why a jump in the price of oil can act like a fall in \(\bar{A}\), and use the table “Which way do employment and the real wage move?” of the Model overview to say what the flexible-price labor market predicts.

  3. In 1981–82 the Federal Reserve tightened money until the federal funds rate approached 20 percent, and unemployment reached nearly 11 percent late in 1982 (Federal Reserve History). Which row of the same table fits 1982? Why did the raw Solow residual fall that year anyway?

  4. What do the two years say about the claim that TFP shocks drive business cycles?

Hint

Equation (4) says raw residual = true TFP growth + utilization growth, so subtract. For (b), think about what the same workers and machines can produce once energy is much more expensive. For (c), a monetary contraction is a monetary expansion run in reverse; which friction lets money change employment?

Your answer:

Solution

(a) From equation (4), \(g_A = (\text{raw residual}) - g_u\):

  • 1974: \(g_A = -3.72 - (-2.62) = -1.10\) percent (Fernald’s adjusted series has \(-1.09\); the identity holds only approximately for annual averages);
  • 1982: \(g_A = -2.76 - (-2.94) = +0.18\) percent.

True TFP fell in 1974 and was roughly flat in 1982, although the raw residual fell in both years.

(b) Output in equation (2) is value added: what capital and labor produce beyond the materials and energy that firms buy. When oil costs nearly four times as much, firms use less of it and switch to slower, less energy-intensive ways of working, and some energy-hungry machines stop paying their way. The same \(K\) and \(L\) then produce less value added, which the model reads as a lower \(\bar{A}\). With flexible prices, labor demand shifts down: employment and the real wage both fall, the first row of the table. This is the real business cycle story, and in 1974 it fits: true TFP fell by about 1.1 percent in a recession year.

(c) A monetary contraction with sticky prices: the output demanded falls, the vertical labor demand curve of equation (9) shifts left, and employment and the real wage both fall (the “monetary expansion, sticky prices” row, in reverse). The sticky-wage row, run in reverse, fits as well: with nominal wages stuck, a lower price level raises the real wage \(\bar{W}/P\), and firms hire fewer workers. Either way a nominal rigidity lets money cut employment, and TFP plays no role. The raw residual fell by 2.76 percent only because utilization fell by 2.94 percent: firms kept workers and machines on hand but ran them less intensively, and equation (3) counts that as lost productivity.

(d) The evidence is mixed. Some recessions, like 1974, come with a true fall in TFP; others, like 1982, have flat TFP and a clear monetary cause. Measured with the raw residual, both years look like TFP recessions, which is why the first RBC models looked so successful. A model of the cycle needs both TFP shocks and monetary shocks with nominal rigidities: the two flavors that modern DSGE models combine.

Problem 3 (Challenge): How elastic must labor supply be? Economists measure how strongly hours respond to a temporary change in the wage, holding consumption fixed, with the Frisch elasticity \(\eta\). Chetty, Guren, Manoli and Weber (NBER Working Paper 16729) note that business-cycle models need much larger labor supply elasticities than studies of individual workers find; their synthesis of the micro evidence points to Frisch elasticities of about 0.5 for the hours of people who work and 0.25 for the decision to work at all.

  1. Show that the labor supply curve (6) has a Frisch elasticity of 1.

  2. Replace the disutility of work in the household’s utility by \(\frac{\eta}{\eta+1}\,\bar{\ell}^{-1/\eta}L^{(\eta+1)/\eta}\). Derive the new labor supply curve and check that it is equation (6) when \(\eta = 1\). Then solve the labor market with labor demand (5) and no tax, and show that the elasticity of \(L^*\) with respect to \(\bar{A}\) is \(3\eta/(3+\eta)\).

  3. In Fernald’s data for 1950–2025, the growth of hours worked has a standard deviation of 2.57 percentage points and the growth of utilization-adjusted TFP one of 1.40 points (files tfp_inputs.csv and tfp_annual.csv, from the Federal Reserve Bank of San Francisco). If TFP shocks in the flexible-price labor market were the only reason hours move, how large would \(\eta\) have to be? Compare it with the micro estimate of 0.5 and with the chapter’s \(\eta = 1\).

Hint
  1. Take logs of equation (6) and change \(\ln w\) with \(c\) fixed. (b) The derivative of the new disutility with respect to \(L\) is \((L/\bar{\ell})^{1/\eta}\); set it equal to \(w/c\). Then repeat steps 1–4 of the labor market’s “Solving the model”, with the power \(1/\eta\) in place of 1. (c) If \(\ln L\) always moves \(\epsilon\) times as much as \(\ln\bar{A}\), its standard deviation is \(\epsilon\) times as large. Solve \(3\eta/(3+\eta) = \epsilon\) for \(\eta\).

Your answer:

# Your answer here
Solution

(a) Taking logs of (6), \(\ln L^s = \ln\bar{\ell} + \ln w - \ln c\). With \(c\) fixed, a 1 percent higher wage raises \(\ln L^s\) by 1 percent: \(\partial\ln L^s/\partial\ln w = 1\), so the Frisch elasticity is 1.

(b) Utility is now \(U = \ln c - \frac{\eta}{\eta+1}\bar{\ell}^{-1/\eta}L^{(\eta+1)/\eta}\), with \(c = wL - \bar{S}\). The power rule brings down \((\eta+1)/\eta\), which cancels the factor in front, and lowers the power by one, to \(1/\eta\):

\[\frac{dU}{dL} = \frac{w}{c} - \bar{\ell}^{-1/\eta}L^{1/\eta} = \frac{w}{c} - \left(\frac{L}{\bar{\ell}}\right)^{1/\eta} = 0 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad L^s = \bar{\ell}\left(\frac{w}{c}\right)^{\eta}.\]

With \(\eta = 1\) the disutility is \(\frac{1}{2}\bar{\ell}^{-1}L^2\) and \(L^s = \bar{\ell}\,w/c\): equation (6). Written as a wage, supply is \(w = c\,(L/\bar{\ell})^{1/\eta}\). Set it equal to labor demand (5):

\[c\,\bar{\ell}^{-1/\eta}L^{1/\eta} = \frac{2}{3}\cdot\frac{\bar{A}K^{1/3}}{L^{1/3}} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad L^{1/\eta + 1/3} = \frac{2}{3}\cdot\frac{\bar{A}K^{1/3}\,\bar{\ell}^{1/\eta}}{c}.\]

The power on the left is \(\frac{1}{\eta} + \frac{1}{3} = \frac{3+\eta}{3\eta}\), so raise both sides to \(\frac{3\eta}{3+\eta}\):

\[L^* = \left[\frac{2}{3}\cdot\frac{\bar{A}K^{1/3}\,\bar{\ell}^{1/\eta}}{c}\right]^{3\eta/(3+\eta)}.\]

In logs, \(\ln L^* = \text{const} + \frac{3\eta}{3+\eta}\ln\bar{A}\): the elasticity is \(3\eta/(3+\eta)\), which is \(3/4\) for \(\eta = 1\), as in the comparative-statics table. It is 0.429 for \(\eta = 0.5\) and 1.5 for \(\eta = 3\), and it can never reach 3, however elastic labor supply is: the falling marginal product caps it.

(c) The required elasticity is \(\epsilon = 2.57/1.40 = 1.84\). Solving \(3\eta/(3+\eta) = \epsilon\) gives \(3\eta = \epsilon(3+\eta)\), so \(\eta = 3\epsilon/(3-\epsilon) = 4.7\). That is nearly ten times the micro estimate of 0.5. With \(\eta = 0.5\), TFP shocks would move hours with a standard deviation of only \(0.429 \times 1.40 = 0.60\) points, under a quarter of the 2.57 in the data; with the chapter’s \(\eta = 1\), about \(0.75 \times 1.40 = 1.05\) points. Problem 4 adds a second difficulty: hours and adjusted TFP do not even move in the same direction.

inputs = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "tfp_inputs.csv")
ratio = inputs.hours_growth.std() / inputs.tfp_util.std()
print(f"standard deviations: hours {inputs.hours_growth.std():.2f}, adjusted TFP {inputs.tfp_util.std():.2f}")
print(f"elasticity needed {ratio:.2f}, so eta = {3 * ratio / (3 - ratio):.1f}")
for eta in (0.5, 1.0, 3.0):
    print(f"eta = {eta}: employment elasticity {3 * eta / (3 + eta):.3f}")

This is the labor-supply puzzle of real business cycle models: to let TFP shocks drive hours, they need labor supply far more elastic than studies of workers find. DSGE models answer with other shocks and with nominal rigidities.

Data-based problems

Problem 4 (Basic): Do hours rise when TFP rises? The file tfp_inputs.csv holds John Fernald’s growth-accounting data for the U.S. business sector, 1950–2025 (Federal Reserve Bank of San Francisco; see the data notes): the growth of output, hours, capital and labor quality, capital’s share, and both TFP measures with utilization. Compute the correlation of hours growth with the raw Solow residual and with utilization-adjusted TFP growth. The flexible-price labor market predicts that hours rise with TFP (an elasticity of 0.75); with sticky prices and unchanged demand, equation (9) predicts that they fall (an elasticity of −3/2). Which prediction do the numbers support, and why do the two TFP measures disagree?

Hint

inputs.hours_growth.corr(inputs.tfp_util) gives one correlation. To see why the measures disagree, also correlate hours with utilization, and remember equation (4).

# Your answer here

Your answer:

Solution

Read the file and compute three correlations:

inputs = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "tfp_inputs.csv")
print(f"hours and raw TFP:      {inputs.hours_growth.corr(inputs.tfp_solow):+.2f}")
print(f"hours and adjusted TFP: {inputs.hours_growth.corr(inputs.tfp_util):+.2f}")
print(f"hours and utilization:  {inputs.hours_growth.corr(inputs.utilization):+.2f}")

Hours growth has a correlation of +0.38 with the raw residual but −0.39 with adjusted TFP. Once utilization is removed, years of fast TFP growth tend to be years in which hours fall. That is the sign that sticky prices predict: when TFP rises and demand does not keep up, firms need fewer workers. Basu, Fernald and Kimball (2006), “Are Technology Improvements Contractionary?”, reach the same answer with careful estimates: inputs fall at first when technology improves, which fits simple sticky-price models but not the standard RBC model.

The raw residual disagrees because it contains utilization (equation 4), and utilization rises and falls with hours: their correlation is +0.65. Firms that hire more also run their workers and machines harder, and plain growth accounting records the extra intensity as higher TFP.

Problem 5 (Intermediate): Growth accounting by hand. Fernald computes the raw Solow residual (tfp_solow) from the columns of tfp_inputs.csv. Rebuild it yourself.

  1. Use equation (3), with the weights 1/3 and 2/3, to compute the residual in every year from output, capital and hours growth; the notebook’s solow_residual function works on whole columns. Compare your residual with tfp_solow in 2009 and 2020.

  2. Over 1950–2025, what are the correlation and the average gap between your residual and Fernald’s?

  3. Fernald’s formula differs from equation (3) in two ways: capital’s share \(\alpha\) is measured every year (capital_share), and labor input also grows with labor quality \(g_q\) (labor_quality), the skill and experience mix of the hours worked: \(g_A = g_Y - \alpha g_K - (1-\alpha)(g_L + g_q)\). Recompute the residual with this formula. How large is the largest gap now?

  4. In which two years did labor quality grow fastest, and why might it jump in those years?

Hint

solow_residual(inputs.gdp_growth, inputs.capital_growth, inputs.hours_growth) returns a whole column; store it as a new column. inputs.year.isin([2009, 2020]) picks the two years, and .nlargest(3, "labor_quality") the years with the fastest labor-quality growth. Look at hours growth in those years.

# Your answer here
Solution 
inputs = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "tfp_inputs.csv")
inputs["simple"] = solow_residual(inputs.gdp_growth, inputs.capital_growth, inputs.hours_growth)
alpha = inputs.capital_share
inputs["full"] = (inputs.gdp_growth - alpha * inputs.capital_growth
                  - (1 - alpha) * (inputs.hours_growth + inputs.labor_quality))
print(inputs[inputs.year.isin([2009, 2020])][["year", "simple", "full", "tfp_solow"]].round(2).to_string(index=False))
gap = inputs.simple - inputs.tfp_solow
print(f"equation (3): correlation {inputs.simple.corr(inputs.tfp_solow):.3f}, average gap {gap.mean():.2f}")
print(f"with alpha and labor quality: largest gap {(inputs.full - inputs.tfp_solow).abs().max():.2f}")
print(inputs.nlargest(3, "labor_quality")[["year", "hours_growth", "labor_quality"]].to_string(index=False))

(a) In 2009, equation (3) gives \(-3.75 - \tfrac{1}{3}\times 1.76 - \tfrac{2}{3}\times(-7.74) = +0.82\) percent with these rounded numbers (+0.83 from the unrounded data), against Fernald’s −0.15; in 2020 it gives +1.27 against −0.23. In both deep recessions the simple formula even turns the sign.

(b) Over all 76 years the two residuals have a correlation of 0.988, but the simple one is on average 0.23 points higher.

(c) With the measured capital share and labor quality, the residual is −0.25 in 2009 and −0.29 in 2020, and the largest gap in any year is 0.10 points; it is not zero only because the identity is exact for quarterly data and approximate for annual averages. Most of the average gap of (b) is labor quality: it grows by 0.38 percent a year on average, and equation (3) leaves its contribution, \(\tfrac{2}{3} \times 0.38 = 0.25\), inside TFP.

(d) The fastest years are 2020 (1.63 percent) and 2009 (1.19 percent), the two years in which hours fell by about 7.7 percent. Labor quality weights each hour by what that kind of worker earns. When it jumps, the hours of less experienced and lower-paid workers have fallen much more than the others, so the average quality of the hours still worked rises. Without that correction, equation (3) counts the better mix of workers as higher TFP.

Problem 6 (Challenge): Is the United States an exception? In Fig. 1’s “Beyond the United States” chart, the Penn World Table 11.0 TFP of the United States fell in only half of its years of falling GDP, while most countries’ TFP fell almost every time.

  1. For each of the 120 countries in pwt_growth.csv, compute the correlation between GDP growth and TFP growth over all of its years, and collect the results in a table.

  2. What is the median correlation? Where does the United States rank, counting from the lowest? Which five countries have the lowest correlations?

  3. Compute the median correlation in each region. Which region stands out?

  4. Does a high correlation show that TFP shocks cause booms and recessions? Use equation (4) and Problem 4.

Hint

Loop over sorted(pwt.country.unique()), keep one country’s rows, and compute .corr() of its two columns; append a small dictionary per country to a list and turn the list into a DataFrame with pd.DataFrame(rows). Then .sort_values("r"), .median() and .groupby("region").

# Your answer here

Your answer:

Solution 
pwt = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "pwt_growth.csv")
rows = []
for country in sorted(pwt.country.unique()):
    data = pwt[pwt.country == country]
    rows.append({"country": country, "region": data.region.iloc[0], "years": len(data),
                 "r": data.gdp_growth.corr(data.tfp_growth)})
table = pd.DataFrame(rows).sort_values("r")
us_r = table[table.country == "United States"].r.iloc[0]
print(f"median correlation {table.r.median():.2f}; United States {us_r:.2f}, "
      f"rank {(table.r < us_r).sum() + 1} of {len(table)} from the lowest")
print(table.head(5).round(2).to_string(index=False))
print(table.groupby("region").r.median().round(2).sort_values())

rows.append({...}) adds one dictionary, one row of the future table, to the list. .iloc[0] takes the first value of a column.

(b) The median correlation is 0.86: in most countries measured TFP rises and falls almost one for one with GDP. The United States, at 0.70, ranks 15th of 120 from the lowest. The five lowest are Serbia (0.18, with only 29 years of data), Tanzania (0.45), Colombia (0.51), Canada (0.56) and South Africa (0.59).

(c) North America, that is Canada and the United States, has a median of 0.63; every other region lies between 0.83 and 0.91. So the United States is unusual, but not alone: its neighbor is even lower.

(d) No. PWT’s TFP is a raw Solow residual, and by equation (4) it contains the change in utilization. Whenever GDP falls for any reason (less demand, tighter credit, a monetary contraction), firms use their workers and machines less intensively, and the residual falls with GDP. The correlation can therefore run from GDP to measured TFP, not from TFP to GDP. For the United States, the one country here with a utilization-adjusted series, Problem 4 found that adjusted TFP and hours move in opposite directions.

Modeling problems

Problem 7 (Basic): Could a fall in TFP explain 2020? In 2020 U.S. business output fell by 2.90 percent, while Fernald’s utilization-adjusted TFP rose by 1.81 percent (tfp_annual.csv). Feed this measured shock into the flexible-price labor market: move the slider from the baseline \(\bar{A} = 1\) to the 2020 level \(\bar{A}' = 1.0181\), as close as the slider allows, and read employment, the real wage and output in the title. Does the model predict a recession or a boom? By how many percentage points does its change in output miss the measured −2.90 percent, and what does that say about the shocks behind the 2020 recession?

Python note. fixed(C_BAR) holds an argument at one value, so interact draws no slider for it.

Hint

At the baseline, TFP and output are both 1, so an output of 1.05 in the title would mean 5 percent more output than before the shock. Compare the sign of the model’s change with the sign in the data first, then the size. The title rounds to two decimals; for more, use equilibrium(A=...) and output(L, A).

interact(labor_market,
         A=FloatSlider(value=1.0, min=0.9, max=1.1, step=0.005, readout_format=".3f", description="TFP Ā",
                       style=WIDE),
         c=fixed(C_BAR), ell=fixed(ELL_BAR));

Source. The model of Fig. 2 above, adapted from Fig. 15.2 in Jones (2024), Macroeconomics, 6th ed.

# Your answer here
Solution

The closest slider value is \(\bar{A} = 1.020\). The title reads employment 1.01, a real wage of 0.68 and output 1.03: the model predicts a boom, with more jobs, higher wages and more output. The functions give the exact numbers:

L_2020, w_2020 = equilibrium(A=1.0181)       # the measured rise of 1.81 percent
Y_2020 = output(L_2020, 1.0181)
print(f"TFP 1.0181: employment {L_2020:.4f}, real wage {w_2020:.4f}, output {Y_2020:.4f}")
print(f"Output: model {100 * (Y_2020 - 1):+.2f}%, data -2.90%, a miss of {100 * (Y_2020 - 1) + 2.90:.2f} points")

With \(\bar{A}' = 1.0181\), employment is 1.0135, the real wage 0.6757 and output 1.0273: output rises by 2.73 percent, about 3/2 times the rise in TFP. Measured output fell by 2.90 percent, so the model misses by 5.63 percentage points, and in the wrong direction. A TFP shock cannot explain the pandemic recession: the fall in output must have come from other shocks, to the supply of labor and to spending.

Problem 8 (Intermediate): How large is the spending multiplier with flexible prices? A government raises its purchases by \(\Delta G\), paid for with taxes. Households, poorer over their lifetimes, cut consumption, and as in Fig. 5 they work more. The multiplier \(\Delta Y/\Delta G\) is the rise in output per unit of extra purchases. The sliders below set \(\Delta G\) and the share of it that households cut from consumption: 1 for a permanent rise, less for a temporary one.

  1. For a permanent rise of \(\Delta G = 0.1\), what are employment, output and the multiplier?

  2. Keep \(\Delta G = 0.1\). What is the smallest share on the slider that gives a multiplier of at least 0.8? Then find the exact share with the output formula of (a). Is a program with that share closer to a permanent or to a temporary rise in purchases?

  3. Ramey (2011) concludes that the multiplier for a temporary, deficit-financed rise in purchases is probably between 0.8 and 1.5 (Journal of Economic Literature). Can the flexible-price model deliver that? What would you add to it?

Python note. The widget cell defines a small function that sets consumption from the two sliders, redraws Fig. 2’s diagram with labor_market, and then replaces its title with fig.update_layout(title=...).

Hint

Consumption is \(c' = 0.6 - \text{share} \times \Delta G\). Output changes only through employment, because \(\bar{A}\) and \(K\) do not move. For (b), raise the share one step at a time and watch the multiplier in the title. For the exact share, work backward: first the output that a multiplier of 0.8 requires, then the consumption that gives that output.

def spending_multiplier(G_rise=0.1, share=1.0):
    """Figs. 2 and 5 again: purchases rise by G_rise and consumption falls by share x G_rise."""
    c_new = C_BAR - share * G_rise
    L_base, w_base = equilibrium()
    L_new, w_new = equilibrium(c=c_new)
    multiplier = (output(L_new) - output(L_base)) / G_rise
    fig = labor_market(c=c_new)
    fig.update_layout(title=f"Employment {L_new:.2f}, output {output(L_new):.2f}, "
                            f"multiplier ΔY/ΔG = {round(multiplier, 2) + 0.0:.2f}")
    return fig


interact(spending_multiplier,
         G_rise=FloatSlider(value=0.1, min=0.02, max=0.2, step=0.02, description="rise in purchases ΔG", style=WIDE),
         share=FloatSlider(value=1.0, min=0.0, max=1.0, step=0.1, description="share cut from consumption",
                           style=WIDE));

Source. The model of Figs. 2 and 5 above, adapted from Figs. 15.2 and 15.5 in Jones (2024), Macroeconomics, 6th ed.

Your answer:

Solution 
L_base, w_base = equilibrium()
for share in (1.0, 0.8, 0.9, 0.3):
    L_new, w_new = equilibrium(c=C_BAR - share * 0.1)
    multiplier = (output(L_new) - output(L_base)) / 0.1
    print(f"share {share}: employment {L_new:.3f}, output {output(L_new):.3f}, "
          f"multiplier {round(multiplier, 2) + 0.0:.2f}")
c_exact = C_BAR / 1.08 ** 2                  # the consumption that gives output 1.08
print(f"A multiplier of 0.8 needs c' = {c_exact:.3f}, a share of {(C_BAR - c_exact) / 0.1:.2f}")

(a) A permanent rise cuts consumption from 0.6 to 0.5. By equation (7), employment rises to \((0.6/0.5)^{3/4} = 1.147\), and output to \((0.6/0.5)^{1/2} = 1.095\). The multiplier is \((1.095 - 1)/0.1 = 0.95\).

(b) On the slider, a share of 0.8 gives a multiplier of 0.74 and a share of 0.9 gives 0.85, so 0.9 is the smallest share that reaches 0.8. Exactly: a multiplier of 0.8 needs output \(1 + 0.8 \times 0.1 = 1.08\). By (a), output is \((0.6/c')^{1/2}\), so \(c' = 0.6/1.08^2 = 0.514\), and the share is \((0.6 - 0.514)/0.1 = 0.86\). Households must cut their consumption by 86 percent of the extra purchases, almost as much as for a permanent rise. With flexible prices, extra purchases raise output only through the wealth effect: people work more because they feel poorer.

(c) No. For a temporary rise, the case Ramey studies, households lose little lifetime income, so they cut consumption by much less than the 86 percent of (b), and the flexible-price multiplier stays far below 0.8: with a share of 0.3 it is only 0.26, and less the shorter the program. Only a permanent, tax-financed rise gets close to 1, and then consumption and the real wage fall. To reach a multiplier near 1 for a temporary program, add sticky prices: firms then produce whatever is demanded, so the extra purchases raise output directly, as in Fig. 8. The estimated Smets–Wouters model, which has sticky prices, finds a multiplier of about 1 (the note after Fig. 5).

Problem 9 (Intermediate): One employment target, two frictions. The central bank wants a monetary expansion that raises employment by 10 percent. How large must the expansion be, and what happens to the real wage,

  1. when nominal wages are sticky at \(\bar{W} = 0.75\), as in Figs. 6–7, starting from point \(A\) with employment 0.70 (the expansion raises the price level by size percent);

  2. when prices are sticky, as in Fig. 8, starting from \(Y_0 = 1\) (the expansion raises the output demanded by size percent)?

  3. Which case is better for the workers who already have a job, and which looks more like an actual boom?

Get close with the sliders, then find the exact answers with the model’s equations.

Hint

With sticky wages, firms are on their labor demand curve, and employment grows with the cube of the price level (the Model overview’s sticky-wage block). With sticky prices, use equation (9) with \(\bar{A} = K = 1\). Set each employment ratio equal to 1.1 and solve for \(P'\) and \(Y'\).

def expansion(friction="sticky wages", size=3.0):
    """Figs. 7 and 8 again: prices (sticky wages) or the output demanded (sticky prices) rise by size percent."""
    if friction == "sticky wages":
        return sticky_wages(t=1, P_new=1 + size / 100, W_bar=0.75)
    fig = sticky_prices(Y_new=1 + size / 100, c_new=C_BAR)
    for trace in fig.data:
        if trace.text == ("A",):
            trace.textposition = "top left"      # keeps the letter A clear of a nearby point B
    return fig


interact(expansion,
         friction=ToggleButtons(options=["sticky wages", "sticky prices"], value="sticky wages",
                                description="friction"),
         size=FloatSlider(value=3.0, min=2.0, max=10.0, step=0.5, readout_format=".1f",
                          description="size of the expansion (percent)", style=WIDE));

Source. The models of Figs. 7 and 8 above, adapted from Figs. 15.7 and 15.8 in Jones (2024), Macroeconomics, 6th ed.

# Your answer here

Your answer:

Solution

(a) Along labor demand, \(L^d = \left[\tfrac{2}{3}\big/(\bar{W}/P')\right]^3 = (P')^3 L^d(\bar{W})\), so employment rises by 10 percent when \((P')^3 = 1.1\), that is \(P' = 1.1^{1/3} = 1.032\): prices must rise by about 3.2 percent. On the slider, 3 percent gives employment 0.77. The real wage falls from 0.75 to \(0.75/1.032 = 0.727\), by 3.1 percent.

(b) By equation (9), \(L = (Y')^{3/2}\), so \((Y')^{3/2} = 1.1\) gives \(Y' = 1.1^{2/3} = 1.066\): the output demanded must rise by 6.6 percent (on the slider, 6.5 percent already gives employment 1.10). The real wage lies on the supply curve, \(w = cL/\bar{\ell}\), so it rises by the same 10 percent, from 0.667 to 0.733.

P_new = 1.1 ** (1 / 3)
L_A, L_B = labor_demand(0.75), labor_demand(0.75 / P_new)
print(f"Sticky wages: P' = {P_new:.4f}, employment {L_A:.3f} -> {L_B:.3f}, real wage 0.750 -> {0.75 / P_new:.3f}")
Y_new = 1.1 ** (2 / 3)
L_sticky = labor_needed(Y_new)
print(f"Sticky prices: Y' = {Y_new:.4f}, employment 1.000 -> {L_sticky:.3f}, "
      f"real wage {supply_wage(1.0):.3f} -> {supply_wage(L_sticky):.3f}")

(c) With sticky wages the new jobs are paid for by everyone who already works: their real wage falls by 3.1 percent. With sticky prices employment and the real wage rise together, by 10 percent each, as they tend to do in actual booms. The two pushes differ in size for two reasons. Prices need to rise by only 3.2 percent because labor demand is very elastic: firms hire about 3 percent more for each 1 percent fall in the real wage. Output demanded must rise by 6.6 percent, two thirds of the employment gain, because \(Y = L^{2/3}\): each extra worker adds less output than the last.

Problem 10 (Challenge): A TFP shock or a tax-like wedge in 2009? In 2009, hours worked in the U.S. business sector fell by 7.74 percent and output by 3.75 percent, while utilization-adjusted TFP rose by 3.53 percent (tfp_inputs.csv). Chari, Kehoe and McGrattan (2007) showed that many frictions act in a growth model like time-varying wedges that resemble taxes on labor or investment (Federal Reserve Bank of Minneapolis staff report; published in Econometrica, doi:10.1111/j.1468-0262.2007.00768.x). Jermann and Quadrini (2012) find that tighter financing conditions for firms contributed to the 2008–2009 recession (American Economic Review). In our labor market, the sales tax \(\tau\) is such a wedge.

  1. With the sliders, check that a TFP fall to \(\bar{A}' = 0.90\) with no wedge, and a wedge \(\tau = 0.10\) with TFP unchanged, both lower employment to 0.92, close to the fall in hours of 2009.

  2. For each story, compute the change in output and the measured Solow residual of equation (3), with capital fixed, in percent (100 times the change in the log, as in Fernald’s data).

  3. Which story fits the 2009 data better?

  4. Suppose the wedge comes from expensive credit: firms must borrow to pay wages before they sell their output. Which policies would raise employment in that case, and why would they do little against a true fall in TFP?

Hint

Only the product \((1-\tau)\bar{A}\) enters equation (7), but output \(Y = \bar{A}K^{1/3}L^{2/3}\) contains \(\bar{A}\) alone. For (b), use equilibrium, output, np.log and solow_residual(g_Y, 0.0, g_L).

interact(labor_shock,
         A_new=FloatSlider(value=1.0, min=0.8, max=1.0, step=0.1, description="TFP after the shock Ā′", style=WIDE),
         tau=FloatSlider(value=0.0, min=0.0, max=0.2, step=0.1, description="tax-like wedge τ", style=WIDE),
         c_new=fixed(C_BAR));

Source. The model of Figs. 3 and 4 above, adapted from Figs. 15.3 and 15.4 in Jones (2024), Macroeconomics, 6th ed.

# Your answer here

Your answer:

Solution

(a) In both cases \((1-\tau)\bar{A} = 0.9\), so equation (7) gives the same point: employment \(0.9^{3/4} = 0.924\) and a real wage of 0.616. The title reads “Employment 1.00 → 0.92, real wage 0.67 → 0.62” for either slider.

(b) Output and the residual differ, because only the TFP story lowers \(\bar{A}\) in the production function:

for A_new, tau in [(0.9, 0.0), (1.0, 0.1)]:
    L_new, w_new = equilibrium(A=A_new, tau=tau)
    g_L = 100 * np.log(L_new)                     # percent, as 100 times the change in the log
    g_Y = 100 * np.log(output(L_new, A_new))
    residual = round(solow_residual(g_Y, 0.0, g_L), 2) + 0.0
    print(f"A = {A_new}, tau = {tau}: employment {g_L:.2f}%, output {g_Y:.2f}%, Solow residual {residual:.2f}%")
Story Employment, percent Output, percent Solow residual, percent
TFP falls to 0.90 −7.90 −15.80 −10.54
wedge \(\tau = 0.10\) −7.90 −5.27 0.00

In the TFP story, \(g_Y = g_A + \tfrac{2}{3}g_L = -10.54 + \tfrac{2}{3}\times(-7.90) \approx -15.8\). In the wedge story, \(\bar{A}\) does not change, so \(g_Y = \tfrac{2}{3}g_L = -5.27\) and the residual is zero.

(c) The wedge story. With hours down by about 8 percent, a TFP recession would have cut output by about 16 percent and measured TFP by more than 10 percent. In 2009 output fell by 3.75 percent, the raw residual by only 0.15 percent, and adjusted TFP rose. The wedge story gets both facts roughly right: an output fall of about 5 percent (somewhat less in the data, because capital still grew by 1.76 percent) and no fall in TFP.

(d) If the wedge is expensive credit, policies that make borrowing cheaper or easier lower \(\tau\) and shift labor demand back up: lower interest rates, central bank lending to banks and firms, loan guarantees, or rebuilding banks’ capital. Against a true TFP fall they would do little, because each worker really produces less: cheaper credit does not raise the marginal product of labor, so firms would still want fewer workers at any given wage.
